Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate because of a vital interest in this topic. For the past few years this matter has been discussed among groups of young people with whom I have met, and I am under an obligation that whenever there was an opportunity in this chamber to discuss the subject I would try to present my personal viewpoint. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) for providing this opportunity this afternoon, because the resolution deals with a pertinent problem in our dominion at the present time.
There have been various attempts during the discussion, which has been quite dispassionate and objective, to place the responsibility for a situation that is all too obvious. We need only look at the bookstands and newspaper stands in our own communities to be aware of the fact that there is a problem. Various speakers this afternoon endeavoured to place the responsibility for this situation. Speaking in broad terms, I believe

the situation arises from the fact that it is possible to commercialize the publication of pornographic literature today. There is a market for that literature, and as long as there is a market of course there will be authors, publishers, distributors and retailers who will be interested in exploiting the market. If I might generalize, I think I would place the responsibility directly on the purchaser, because it is the purchaser who provides the market for this type of literature.
It is a long-established truism that biographies of sinners have always tended to be better sellers than the biographies of saints. Judging by the tremendous turnover in obscene literature and pulp magazines of the pornographic variety, it would seem that a great many people want it that way. They are willing to buy; they are interested in the subject; and they are willing to pay the necessary price for that type of literature. This afternoon we have been dealing largely with the difficulty which arises when this literature becomes available to children and adolescents. From my knowledge of the limited financial resources of this age group it would seem that they are not the chief offenders in creating the demand. I believe it is the purchaser on the adult level who provides the financial stimulus necessary to enable this business to continue quite profitably.
In Maclean's magazine a few months ago there was the biography of one of the more prolific writers in this field of popular fiction, a person by the name of Mickey Spillane. I was interested in the article because Maclean's is a reputable publication and always presents a factual case. I was surprised to discover that some 7 million copies of the Spillane type of murder mystery had been sold on the North American continent. Canada would, of course, be part of that market. One can see the Spillane type of murder mystery, as it is called, on every newsstand, and in almost every instance it is a combination of lechery and violence. The bulk of the purchases of this type of literature is not made by children or adolescents, but by the adult population. It would seem that a good many enjoy that type of escape from reality or that type of release from the confused situation in which they find themselves.
The very fact that there are 7 million readers-and no doubt a greater number have since become fans of the Mickey Spillane novels-would tend to suggest that some of the statements made by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) are correct. What we find confronting us today is a tendency toward a moral breakdown, a failure to distinguish between what is good and what is bad so far as literary values are concerned.
Obscene Literature
In so far as children are concerned, and adolescents who are still dependent upon the home and other social institutions, this problem would be no problem at all if those institutions were exercising the control that they have traditionally exercised. The very fact that moral standards have tended to become dim in the confusion and complexities of modern civilization would suggest that these basic social institutions have lost some of their control over the young people in our society. When I speak of "decline in our moral standards", I mean there is a failure to an increasing degree to distinguish the principles by which we judge behaviour to be either right or wrong.
Arising then from the problem of the market available for this type of literature, it seems to me that the solution put forward in the resolution by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has some validity. I am particularly interested when he speaks of a joint committee of both houses of parliament being set up for the purpose of studying and recommending legislation or other measures. I like the idea of "other measures" perhaps better than recommending legislation. Then the increasing volume of filthy literature circulated in Canada could be dealt with effectively but without, at the same time, improperly restricting the freedom of the press or genuine literary or artistic expression.
The very fact that this discussion has taken place here this afternoon will create an awareness among those who should accept responsibility in this regard. For example, take the recently established organizations existing in a good many of our schools across Canada, the parent-teachers associations. If they were to get hold of the significance and magnitude of this problem it would not be very long before they began to take some positive and constructive action to remedy the situation. I am sure the publicity given to this matter will create such an awareness in places where it does not already exist. Because of the complex nature of the society in which we live, there are all sorts of things going on almost under our noses of which we are not aware until they are actually brought to our attention by someone who is a little more observant, someone who has a keener appreciation of his social and community responsibilities.
In bringing my remarks to a close, I commend the hon. member for Kamloops for providing this opportunity to discuss the subject. I would suggest that once the problem is brought to the attention of those institutions or groups responsible in every part of Canada, it could be dealt with successfully on the local community level. If it

Obscene Literature
goes to a committee, as is suggested in the resolution, and receives further airing and discussion, and if a real awareness of the difficulty is established, then the particular problem that has received the greatest emphasis this afternoon-namely, that of children and adolescents being exposed to obscene literature-will to a large extent wither away.

subtopic: PROPOSED JOINT COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH FILTHY LITERATURE
speechtext:
What brings me into this debate this afternoon is a reference made by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), and some extracts read from the evidence given by Mayor Whitton. There is in my home town a small newsstand, the name of which I have no intention of mentioning here for fear of possible repercussions against it later. I was approached by the proprietor of that little newsstand last summer and he was discussing this question of the sale of various types of what might be called undesirable literature. He informed me, as was stated by the hon. member for Portneuf, that if he wished to obtain a reasonable supply of what he considered were the desirable magazines, a sufficient supply to serve his regular customers, he also had to take so many hundreds of pounds of various types of intellectual tripe.
A lot of the material he would be compelled to take in order to qualify for his quota of better literature was not necessarily pornographic, filthy or illegal, though some of it most likely was. If it is the situation that, in order to get a supply of magazines class A, a retailer has to accept and pay for a given quantity of magazines class B, that is something or other in restraint of or in control of private enterprise. It should be investigated, and most thoroughly investigated, I respectfully submit, by the Department of Justice, and that soon; because I believe that situation is responsible for some, if not all, of the sale of the material which is objected to in the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops.
I must say I have some sympathy for the small businessman who finds himself in that position, who cannot make a working profit and pay for the junk out of the profits he will get from the better class of material, and therefore in self-defence has to display and dispose of the less desirable types of literature.
I have not the slightest doubt that if that situation exists it is going to be pretty difficult to ferret out, because the people who are in business in a big way are by no means ignorant as to how to conceal what they are doing, and those who depend upon them

for their supplies, which means those who depend upon them for their livelihood-I refer to the little retailer-may have some difficulty in producing the necessary evidence upon which to found a case.
With reference to the meat of the hon. member's resolution, in this case I find myself in agreement with much of what has been said by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and I presume that means much of what has been said by the hon. member for Greenwood has merit. In particular he frankly admitted the difficulties in solving what is equally frankly a problem.
The first question that comes to my mind, and which I think has been discussed in a great many homes and a great many other forums, is what is filthy; what is obscene; what is pornographic?
One hon. member, whose name I have forgotten, referred to the evidence before the Senate divorce committees as being this type of filth or pornographic literature. Well, I am wondering. That is a factually documented report, published without the slightest effort being made to make it palatable, to make it good reading. It is just about as sensational, it is just about as attractive, from my point of view, as a medical book on some branch of obstetrics might be, yet it is not desirable reading. It is not the type of thing that the average parent would supply to a twelve-year-old child. Nevertheless it is doubtful whether anyone would say that publication of that particular material should be made illegal.
I honestly believe that if we took all the members of this house of one political group -I do not care which-we could produce to them certain types of doubtful literature and find that some would regard it as pornographic and illegal and worthy of suppression, while others would regard it as of no importance at all. There is of course no question that certain types of material are definitely pornographic, flagrantly so, while others are not. But there is this dividing line somewhere, and the whole crux of the question is that nobody can agree just where it is.
Then I think the question has been somewhat bemused this afternoon with the addition of a great many references to what is intellectually desirable. I think it was the hon. member for Greenwood who described it as trivial and worthless. I feel-and I do not know that I am too much of a highbrow- that a great deal of the material which is now being sold in bookstores and other places is trivial and is intellectual tripe; but I would not have the slightest excuse for suggesting that it was immoral or should be

made illegal. Perhaps it is a fair comparison to say that there are a lot of very cheap candies on sale which do not do the children who buy them any good and which do not do them any harm, except that when they are taking these cheap and worthless candies they are filling their little stomachs with stuff which will do them much less good than if they were getting good fresh fruit, or something of that sort. In other words, it may not do them any positive harm, but it is keeping out the possibility of doing a certain amount of positive good. If you were to carry that analogy further down the line of course you would come to the material which would actually poison the child, and we are dealing now with the material which will poison the minds not the reading of which is just a very silly waste of time.
Then there is the other question. Perhaps I am a little bit old-fashioned. I am not one of those-at least I do not think I am

who rush in to the defence of advanced thought along most any line except of course political; but we have to be just a little careful that in our discussion of this or any other similar matter we do not decide that the stage at which we have arrived, you and I, is the ultimate; that because we have said, or have decided in our own minds, that this is good and that is bad, you shall not go any farther; that this decision, like the law of the Medes and Persians, can never be changed.
I wonder if I may be permitted to use an example that I know full well is a most dangerous one. There are in the house and country hundreds of thousands of people who are quite morally convinced that anything dealing with free information on the subject of birth control is absolutely immoral. There are also in this country, and most likely in the House of Commons, a great number of people who are quite firmly and morally convinced that the advocacy of birth control is something which is morally right and, some people think, morally desirable. I am not going to say who is right; that is not the question before us. The point is that there can be very firm convictions held by very decent people as to what is right and what is wrong; yet the convictions of one group can be anathema to the other group.
That brings me to an observation made by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). He was dealing with the possibility of some form of censorship or control, and his words as I took note of them were: "The law can never be too severe". That is something with which I cannot agree, because 1 think conceivably it could be. If the law were imposed by a group of intellectuals
Obscene Literature
whose views were different from mine, I would then be of the opinion that the law was too severe. A form of control based upon what we are led to believe was the official thinking of the Puritans on the North American continent, in the early days, might be acceptable to some in this country and quite unacceptable to others. Yet both groups might be perfectly decent and Christian, and equally sincere.
If I remember correctly it was the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) who made what I believe, thus far, has been the only positive approach to the subject. All the rest of us have been talking from the negative viewpoint, stating that something should be forbidden. While I do not undertake at the moment to offer my support to the hon. member's suggestion, the fact is that he did make one concrete and positive suggestion as to the manner in which the problem might be met.
I think all of us have been thinking in terms that are purely negative. The solution facing us at the moment would appear to me -and conceivably I could be wrong-to be that we are going to have decisions as to what is or what is not to be sold made either by some board of censors or under the Criminal Code. I do not think anyone will claim that, to date, the results in the criminal courts have been satisfactory. I lay part of the blame where I placed it when I began these observations, namely on the situation which I believe exists as between distributors and retailers. But we are told by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) today that we may expect a good deal from the disposition of a case now under appeal.
I am afraid of a board of censors. Quite frankly I am afraid of anyone undertaking to tell me what shall be my standards in respect of morals or decency. I would be afraid to place the matter under the control of a board of censors which, if it wished, could tell us that the statue of Venus de Milo is indecent and immoral, and that every reproduction of it should be removed. Then, if it went too far the other way, quite conceivably it could continue to permit the importation and sale in this country of some things which would be offensive to a great majority of the people.

Does the remark the hon. member has just made indicate that he would favour doing away

with censorship or quasi-censorship such as I understand exists through the customs, against this kind of literature?

subtopic: PROPOSED JOINT COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH FILTHY LITERATURE
speechtext:
If any alternative solution at all can be found within the Criminal Code or elsewhere my present answer would be yes. I was just going to deal with that. I do not believe that any group of individuals, whether set up as a board of censorship under a provincial government or whether it be a branch of the Department of National Revenue, or whether it be set up under some new act of parliament, should decide what shall and what shall not be literature.
I do not believe any such board of censors could come to a decision that would meet with the approval-I do not say the pleasure -of the majority of people in this country; because I do firmly hold the view that the standards and tastes of all of us vary to such an extent that no 20 people, or no 262 people, can say what is or what is not going to be effective. They must draw the line somewhere, putting things on one side or on the other.
There is only one alternative solution that I can see. It may not be perfect, and I know that there are weaknesses in it. The alleged crime would have to occur, followed by a decision by jurists. If they came to a conclusion that just looking at a picture would have an immoral effect, and that it should be removed, their decision would have to be respected. I know there are weaknesses in this alternative, in that a certain amount of damage is done before a decision is made. But, speaking as one individual who must choose between that and living under the jurisdiction of one or several boards of censors, I will choose the criminal court solution every time.

subtopic: PROPOSED JOINT COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH FILTHY LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate because I have received several letters from people in my constituency. Then, a year ago samples of some books were sent to me. If I had my way and it were possible to have these objectionable books taken off the shelves of the bookstores in Canada, I would certainly have it done.
The books to which I have referred were received from a Christian lady. I gathered from her letter that she had read them. I read them, and having done so carried them over to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who, I hope, in turn also read them. In this way we have gained firsthand knowledge of some of the vicious literature contained within the covers of these novels. I was not afraid the books would do the minister any

harm, because I felt his age and experience would protect him. I was sure they would not hurt him physically, mentally or morally.
If the appointment of a commission should be the right procedure in this matter, I would be in favour of it. On the other hand it occurs to me that a board of censors-and when I say this I realize I am disagreeing with the hon. member who preceded, me in the debate -might be the better alternative.
Any move to clear out this vicious literature and make it less easily obtainable by our young people is a move in the right direction. The vicious contents of this literature, the suggestive names the books carry and the luxurious pictures on their covers in my opinion are not good for the younger people of Canada. If this resolution is a move in the right direction I am in favour of it.

subtopic: PROPOSED JOINT COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH FILTHY LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) upon his thorough preparation and presentation. This question of obscene literature does not alarm me so much today as it did two years ago, because I am told by booksellers that there is a greater demand today, not for literature dealing with the breaking of the seventh commandment but for a better type of book. There are many books dealing with the way a man can overcome his worries, how men and women can carry out their tasks in life and win the victory.
The writings of Lloyd Douglas are in great demand. He is an outstanding guide and helper. The demand today for his books and his type of literature is much greater than it was a few years ago. Dr. Norman Peel of New York is an outstanding writer who tells men and women how they can best overcome their worries and achieve a clean life. I have some pamphlets here which indicate the type of literature available. This indicates that there is inspiration everywhere; it tells us to let freedom reign, how to become secure in insecure times and so on. As our church leaders, our doctors, our teachers, our members of legislatures advertise these things through their own lives, the great call will not be for literature dealing with the breaking of the seventh commandment.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said that there is enough legislation if it is enforced. I do not know whether this resolution will help, but if we can get something that will be enforced I think we should have it. In your prayer every day you say, "lead us not into temptation." If this committee were set up it might show the booksellers and those who would appear before it the

error of their ways, and they might wake up. You cannot make people good by passing resolutions or legislation; the change must be in their own hearts.

subtopic: PROPOSED JOINT COMMITTEE TO RECOMMEND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH FILTHY LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the comments of the various hon. members who have spoken on this important resolution. Members of the Social Credit group I believe will support the resolution. There is great difficulty in knowing just how to correct the problem which is involved. Everyone knows that for some strange reason obscenity seems to be increasing in the literature commonly available to people. How to stop that increase, how to take the necessary steps to restore the standards of high thinking which prevailed fifty years ago, is something which I think is beyond the average mind to conceive.
I can see no harm in calling a committee of this kind and having them devote a measure of attention to possible solutions of the problem. Whether or not any legislation would be based on their findings that would be of assistance, I would hate to say. But I do believe we ought to do everything we can. If we do not do everything we can to improve the moral attitude of the youth of our time and their elders, I think we shall stand condemned before those who follow.
